content: The World Health Organization (WHO) secretariat reviewed the declarations submitted and found no significant financial, commercial, or intellectual conflicts of interest. Consequently, it determined that no member should be excluded from actively participating in the formulation of recommendations. The secretariat was satisfied with the transparency of the declarations of interest provided by the external review group, and no exclusions were deemed necessary. During a session on guideline development methods convened by the Guideline Review Committee secretariat at the virtual meeting of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) in September 2020, all participants verbally disclosed any potential conflicts of interest. The evidence review team was contracted through the Cochrane Collaboration under specific terms of reference. Researchers involved in the review were required to complete WHO declaration of interest forms, which were subsequently assessed and cleared by the WHO secretariat for any financial, commercial, or intellectual conflicts of interest. Two GDG members who contributed to studies addressing PICO 2 did not participate in discussions related to PICO 2. Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), also known as kala-azar, is the most severe form of leishmaniasis, a systemic protozoan parasitic disease. Without timely and adequate treatment, VL is fatal. The disease is transmitted through the bite of female sandflies and is primarily caused by Leishmania donovani in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, and Leishmania infantum in the Mediterranean Basin, the Middle East, Central Asia, South America, and Central America. In East Africa and South-East Asia, VL is predominantly transmitted from human to human (anthroponotic), whereas zoonotic transmission (involving animal reservoir hosts) is more common in other regions. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) can occur after successful VL treatment and is most prevalent in the Indian subcontinent and Sudan, with occasional cases in other East African countries. The epidemiology of leishmaniasis is influenced by the characteristics of the parasite species, the local ecology at transmission sites, the human population's exposure history to the parasite, and human behavior. Leishmaniasis can also be transmitted through shared syringes among intravenous drug users, blood transfusion, and congenital transmission from mother to infant, though these modes are less common than vector-borne transmission. VL is known for its high diversity and complexity. In 2020, over 90% of VL cases reported to WHO occurred in Brazil, Ethiopia, Eritrea, India, Iraq, Kenya, Nepal, Somalia, South Sudan, and Sudan. These high-burden countries are among the more than 70 countries where VL is considered endemic. Global incidence estimates indicate a decline in VL cases over the past decade, from 200,000–400,000 new cases in 2012 to 50,000–90,000 in 2016. During the early 2000s, Bangladesh, India, and Nepal collectively accounted for more than 50% of the global VL burden. In 2005, these countries signed an agreement to eliminate VL as a public health problem by 2015, targeting an annual incidence of less than one case per 10,000 people at the district (Nepal) and subdistrict (India and Bangladesh) levels. The target date was later revised to 2020. While incidence on the Indian subcontinent has sharply decreased, East Africa has become the largest focus, with an increasing proportion of global VL cases and recurrent epidemics. Risk factors for progression to VL and increased spread in all transmission settings include malnutrition, genetic factors, population movement, other infectious diseases, and immune suppression, particularly HIV infection. HIV remains a major global public health issue, having claimed nearly 33 million lives to date, with an estimated 38 million people living with HIV at the end of 2019. By mid-2020, 26 million people had access to antiretroviral therapy (ART), representing 67% of those living with HIV who knew their status. HIV prevalence in the general population of East Africa and South-East Asia is generally low, but increasing numbers of new infections have been reported in certain population groups. Early access to ART and support for treatment adherence are critical not only to improve the health of people living with HIV but also to prevent HIV transmission. However, success varies by region, country, and population, as access to HIV testing, treatment, and care is not yet universal. Marginalized populations at risk of VL, such as migrants and seasonal workers from Ethiopia and India, are particularly vulnerable due to limited access to VL and HIV services. HIV and Leishmania infections exacerbate each other, worsening patient outcomes. The geographical overlap of HIV and Leishmania endemicity has progressively increased over the past few decades. Since the first case was reported in 1985, 45 countries have documented HIV–Leishmania coinfection. VL is included in WHO’s clinical staging system for HIV as a stage 4 AIDS-defining condition (atypical disseminated leishmaniasis). In southern Europe, up to 70% of adult VL cases are associated with HIV infection, although the number of new cases has decreased since the late 1990s, primarily due to ART access. In other parts of the world with limited access to ART, prevalence is steadily rising. Northern Ethiopia has a particularly high rate of HIV infection among VL patients, ranging from 15–35%. HIV testing among VL patients in India has recently been significantly scaled up. Data reported to WHO from 2014–2020 showed that over 50,000 people with VL were tested for HIV in 16 countries, and 3,070 cases (new and relapses) of VL–HIV coinfection were recorded. VL with HIV coinfection has significant epidemiological, clinical, and public health implications for patients, their families, clinical services, and disease control and elimination programs.
